original_question: Is every transfinitely nilpotent connected pro-Lie group pronilpotent?
target_in_paper: Section 9, Question 10: "Is a transfinitely nilpotent connected pro-Lie group pronilpotent?"
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's exact target almost verbatim. It has the correct hypothesis (transfinitely nilpotent), the correct ambient class (connected pro-Lie groups), and the correct conclusion (pronilpotent), without broadening the problem beyond the paper.
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, it should specify the paper's meaning of "pro-Lie group": a topological group isomorphic to a closed subgroup of a product of finite-dimensional real Lie groups; equivalently, by Theorem 8, a projective limit of finite-dimensional Lie groups.

The survey itself does not re-state the formal definition of "transfinitely nilpotent"; it explicitly refers back to [17] for the pro-Lie-group notion. A stand-alone version should indicate that this is the standard transfinite nilpotency notion used in pro-Lie theory.

The survey does not separately re-define the group-level term "pronilpotent" in Section 9; the nearby Lie-theoretic context only re-defines pronilpotence on the pro-Lie algebra side. A stand-alone version should make clear that the term is meant in the standard pro-Lie sense used by the authors.

If one wants to include the immediate hidden context from the paper, one should note that any such group is automatically prosolvable, because transfinitely nilpotent implies transfinitely solvable and the connected solvability equivalence theorem applies.
The Lie-theoretic ambient field is the real numbers, since the paper's pro-Lie groups are built from finite-dimensional real Lie groups and the associated pro-Lie algebras are real.
refined_question: Let G be a connected pro-Lie group in the sense of Hofmann and Morris, i.e. a topological group isomorphic to a closed subgroup of a product of finite-dimensional real Lie groups. If G is transfinitely nilpotent in the standard pro-Lie-theoretic sense used by the authors, must G be pronilpotent?
justification: The draft is targeting the paper's official open problem exactly: it appears as Question 10 in Section 9 with essentially the same wording. To make the question stand-alone, one must import the paper's ambient definition of pro-Lie group from the introduction and Theorem 8, and also note the nearby Lie-theoretic context in Section 6, where pronilpotence is discussed on the pro-Lie algebra side and linked to connected pro-Lie groups through the Lie functor and the functor Γ. The sentence immediately after Question 10 supplies important hidden context: such a group is automatically prosolvable, and the stated obstacle is that transfinite nilpotency is not preserved under quotients.
